lead: This unit is about how one component of a mixture moves through another when a concentration difference exists. You will learn Fick's two laws, use them for steady diffusion in gases, liquids and solids, and handle changing area, many components and changing time. After it you can set up and solve the diffusion problems that absorption, drying, membrane and reactor design rest on.
about: Chapter 1.1 places mass transfer among the separation operations and fixes the vocabulary of phases and compositions. Chapter 1.2 splits the total flux of a species into a diffusion part and a bulk-flow part, so that Fick's law in 1.3 has a clean object to describe. Chapters 1.4 and 1.5 apply the first law to steady cases: stagnant and equimolar diffusion in fluids, then geometry that changes with position and a boundary that moves slowly. Chapter 1.6 shows how D is measured and estimated. Chapter 1.7 carries the same laws into solids, 1.8 extends them to mixtures of three or more species, and 1.9 drops the steady-state assumption. Later units turn these fluxes into coefficients, stages and equipment.

chapters.idea: Mass transfer is the movement of a component because of a concentration difference, and every separation operation is a named way of arranging that movement.
chapters.depth: Define mass transfer and contrast it with heat transfer and fluid flow. Give plant and home examples: drying clothes, CO2 removal from flue gas, sugar recovery from cane, oxygen pickup by blood. Classify by how the second phase is made: phase creation (distillation, evaporation, crystallization), phase addition (absorption, extraction, leaching), a barrier (reverse osmosis, dialysis), a solid agent (adsorption, ion exchange, drying with hot air). Also classify by phases in contact (gas-liquid, liquid-liquid, gas-solid, liquid-solid) and by contactor: stage-wise such as trays versus differential such as packed towers and falling films; batch versus continuous. Define mole fraction y (vapour) and x (liquid), mass fraction, molar concentration c = P/RT for an ideal gas, and molar density for a liquid. Some syllabi head this material 'Principles of mass transfer'. No equipment sizing here.

figure.aria: A classification tree that sorts mass transfer operations into four families by how the second phase is created.

children.label: Phase creation
children.note: heat or work makes a new phase

children.label: Phase addition
children.note: a solvent or gas is added

chapters.example: A flue gas at 1 atm and 300 K contains 22 mol% CO2 and 78 mol% air (take M of air = 29 g/mol, M of CO2 = 44 g/mol, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)). Find (a) the mean molar mass, (b) the mass fraction of CO2, (c) the total concentration c in mol/m3, (d) the mass concentration of CO2 in kg/m3. Solution: M = 0.22×44 + 0.78×29 = 9.68 + 22.62 = 32.3 g/mol. Mass fraction of CO2 = 9.68/32.3 = 0.300. c = P/RT = 101325/(8.314×300) = 40.6 mol/m3. Then c_A = 0.22×40.6 = 8.93 mol/m3 and ρ_A = c_A M_A = 8.93×0.044 = 0.393 kg/m3.
chapters.trap: Writing 'concentration' without saying which one. Mole fraction, mass fraction, mol/m3 and kg/m3 are four different numbers, and a flux computed with the wrong one is off by a factor of the molar mass.
chapters.leave: Absorption to Unit 3, distillation to Unit 4, extraction and leaching to Unit 5, adsorption, ion exchange and membranes to Unit 6, humidification and drying to Unit 7. Mass transfer coefficients to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Each species in a mixture has its own velocity, and the flux of that species splits into a diffusion part measured relative to the mixture and a bulk-flow part carried by the mixture itself.
chapters.depth: Define velocity of species A, v_A (m/s), and concentration c_A, so the molar flux is N_A = c_A v_A in mol/(m2·s). Define the molar average velocity u = Σc_i v_i/c and the mass average velocity. Define the diffusion velocity v_A − u and the diffusion flux J_A = c_A(v_A − u), giving N_A = J_A + y_A(N_A + N_B) for a binary. Name the reference frames: fixed (laboratory) frame for N_A, molar-average frame for J_A, mass-average and volume-average frames. Show that J_A = −J_B in a binary but N_A is not −N_B unless the fluxes are equimolar. State that N_A, n_A (mass flux) and molar and mass fluxes per unit area are different objects and give the conversions. This chapter fixes the language; no law of diffusion yet.

figure.title: From species velocity to total flux
figure.aria: A five-step block chain that starts from measured species velocities and ends with the total molar flux of A written as diffusion flux plus bulk flow.

chapters.example: A binary gas at 300 K and 1 atm has c = 40.6 mol/m3 and y_A = 0.30. The measured molar fluxes are N_A = 3.0×10⁻³ and N_B = 1.0×10⁻³ mol/(m2·s). Find the molar average velocity u, the diffusion flux J_A, the velocity of A and its diffusion velocity. Solution: u = (N_A + N_B)/c = 4.0×10⁻³/40.6 = 9.85×10⁻⁵ m/s. J_A = N_A − y_A(N_A + N_B) = 3.0×10⁻³ − 0.30×4.0×10⁻³ = 1.8×10⁻³ mol/(m2·s). c_A = 0.30×40.6 = 12.18 mol/m3, so v_A = N_A/c_A = 2.46×10⁻⁴ m/s, and v_A − u = 2.46×10⁻⁴ − 9.85×10⁻⁵ = 1.48×10⁻⁴ m/s, which equals J_A/c_A = 1.8×10⁻³/12.18.
chapters.trap: Calling N_A the diffusion flux. When y_A is large the bulk term y_A(N_A + N_B) is a big part of N_A, and setting N_A = J_A gives a wrong D in the next chapter.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for mole fraction and concentration.
chapters.leave: Convective mass transfer, where u is the flow itself, to Unit 2. Interphase transfer to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Fick's first law makes the diffusion flux proportional to the negative concentration gradient, and adding conservation of mass gives the second law, which tells how concentration changes with time.
chapters.depth: State Fick's first law as J_A = −D_AB dc_A/dz, define D_AB (m2/s), explain the minus sign and the units. Give the molar-fraction form J_A = −c D_AB dy_A/dz and the form with the bulk term, N_A = −c D_AB dy_A/dz + y_A(N_A + N_B). Note that for a binary ideal mixture D_AB = D_BA. Derive the second law with a shell balance on a slab: in − out = accumulation, divide by Δz, let Δz → 0, giving ∂c_A/∂t = D_AB ∂²c_A/∂z² for constant D and no reaction; write the version with a reaction term and with D depending on c. List the boundary and initial conditions that make a problem well posed. Define steady state as ∂c_A/∂t = 0, which gives a straight-line profile in a slab. Note the limits: dilute solutions, no convection, no reaction.

figure.title: From first law to second law
figure.aria: A five-step block chain from Fick's first law, through a shell balance and a limit, to Fick's second law and its steady-state form.

chapters.example: In a gas mixture at 1 atm and 300 K, c = 40.6 mol/m3 and D_AB = 1.8×10⁻⁵ m2/s. The mole fraction of A is 0.30 at z = 0 and 0.10 at z = 4 mm. (a) Find the diffusion flux J_A, assuming a straight-line profile. (b) Is a straight line consistent with steady state? Solution: dc_A/dz = c dy_A/dz = 40.6×(0.10 − 0.30)/0.004 = 40.6×(−50) = −2030 mol/m4. J_A = −D_AB dc_A/dz = 1.8×10⁻⁵×2030 = 3.65×10⁻² mol/(m2·s), directed towards increasing z. For steady state ∂c_A/∂t = 0, Fick's second law needs d²c_A/dz² = 0, and a straight line satisfies this exactly.
chapters.trap: Losing the minus sign, or using J_A where the problem asks for N_A through a stagnant gas. Also, D of a gas hardly changes with concentration, but D of a liquid does; do not assume constant D blindly.
chapters.leave: Solutions of the second law for a slab with a convective surface, and drying curves, to Chapter 1.9 and Unit 7. Mass transfer coefficients to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: In equimolar counter-diffusion the flux is driven by the plain mole-fraction difference, while in diffusion through a stagnant B the flux is larger by the factor 1/(y_B)lm because A must drift through B.
chapters.depth: Steady one-dimensional diffusion with constant D and c. Equimolar: N_A = D c (y_A1 − y_A2)/L = −N_B. Stagnant B (A diffusing through a non-diffusing B, as in evaporation into air or absorption with an insoluble carrier): N_A = (D c/L) ln(y_B2/y_B1) = D c (y_A1 − y_A2)/(L (y_B)lm), with (y_B)lm = (y_B2 − y_B1)/ln(y_B2/y_B1). Show the same result as a film model: a gas film of thickness L. For liquids replace c by the solution molar density (about 55 500 mol/m3 for water) and y by x: N_A = (D c/L) ln(x_B2/x_B1). Say what laminar flow conditions mean here (smooth streamlines, no eddies, transport across the stream only by molecular diffusion) and note that a laminar jet or a wetted-wall column is the standard apparatus. Do not derive absorption design.

figure.aria: Mole fraction of A against distance for the worked example: a straight line for equimolar diffusion and a curved line for diffusion through stagnant B, both falling from 0.20 to 0.05 over 5 mm.

chapters.example: A gas at 300 K and 1 atm (c = 40.6 mol/m3) has D_AB = 1.8×10⁻⁵ m2/s. The mole fraction of A is 0.20 at one plane and 0.05 at a plane 5 mm away. Find the flux of A when (a) A and B diffuse in opposite directions in equimolar amounts, (b) B is stagnant. Solution: (a) N_A = D c (y_A1 − y_A2)/L = 1.8×10⁻⁵×40.6×0.15/0.005 = 0.0219 mol/(m2·s). (b) y_B1 = 0.80, y_B2 = 0.95, so (y_B)lm = (0.95 − 0.80)/ln(0.95/0.80) = 0.15/0.1719 = 0.873, and N_A = 0.0219/0.873 = 0.0251 mol/(m2·s). The check by the log form: N_A = (1.8×10⁻⁵×40.6/0.005)×ln(0.95/0.80) = 0.1462×0.1719 = 0.0251 mol/(m2·s).
chapters.trap: Using the equimolar formula when B cannot pass, which is the usual case for evaporation into air or for absorption of a soluble gas from an insoluble carrier. Also using the gas value of c for a liquid; a liquid solution is about a thousand times denser in mol/m3.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.3 for the first law; integration.
chapters.leave: Overall coefficients and the two-resistance theory to Unit 2. Absorber design, HTU and NTU to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: When the cross-section for diffusion changes with position, the total rate is constant but the flux is not, so Fick's law is integrated over the geometry; when the boundary itself moves slowly, each instant can be treated as steady.
chapters.depth: General steady form for constant total rate W (mol/s): W = −D A(z) dc_A/dz, so W∫dz/A = −D∫dc_A. Work the sphere in full: for diffusion from a sphere of radius R into a stagnant medium, W = 4πR D c ln(1/(1 − y_As)); for equimolar diffusion between two spheres W = 4πD(c_A1 − c_A2)/(1/R1 − 1/R2). Mention the cylinder and the cone as the same integration with a different A(z). Explain pseudo-steady state: the amount of material held in the gas phase is tiny compared with what crosses, so the profile adjusts instantly and the rate obeys the steady formula at the current radius. Set up the moving-boundary mass balance: the moles lost by the shrinking phase equal W dt. Cover the subliming ball (or evaporating droplet) and the falling liquid level in a tube, the second being the working principle of the Stefan tube. State when the assumption fails: very short times, very fast changes, a gas that dissolves appreciably.

figure.aria: Radius of a subliming sphere in millimetres falling from 10 mm to 5 mm over about 38 hours as the square root of time.

chapters.example: A naphthalene ball of radius 10 mm sublimes in still air at 300 K and 1 atm (c = 40.6 mol/m3, D = 6.0×10⁻⁶ m2/s). The mole fraction of naphthalene at the surface is 0.0100 and in the bulk air it is zero. M = 128 g/mol, solid density 1140 kg/m3. Find the time for the radius to fall to 5 mm. Solution: pseudo-steady rate W = 4πR D c ln(1/(1 − 0.0100)) = 4πR×6.0×10⁻⁶×40.6×0.01005 = 3.08×10⁻⁶ R mol/s. Moles in the ball N = (4/3)πR³ρ/M, so dN/dt = 4πR²(ρ/M) dR/dt = −W. This gives R dR/dt = −D c L M/ρ = −5.50×10⁻¹⁰ m2/s, where L = ln(1/(1 − y_As)). Integrate: t = (R1² − R2²)ρ/(2 D c L M) = (1.0×10⁻⁴ − 2.5×10⁻⁵)/(2×5.50×10⁻¹⁰) = 1.36×10⁵ s, that is 38 hours.
chapters.trap: Integrating −D dc/dz over a fixed area when the area grows with z, and forgetting that the moving boundary makes t appear through R² − R1², not R − R1.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.4 for the stagnant flux; integration of 1/A.
chapters.leave: Transient diffusion inside a solid pellet to Chapter 1.9. Time lag of membranes to Chapter 1.9.

chapters.idea: D is obtained either by measuring how fast a concentration changes in a known geometry or by predicting it from kinetic theory and group correlations.
chapters.depth: Measurement: the two-bulb (Winkelmann) method for gases, the Stefan tube (a pseudo-steady falling level, Chapter 1.5), the diaphragm cell for liquids, and the closed-cell method; mention Taylor dispersion as a modern method that only a few universities teach. Prediction for gases: Chapman–Enskog with Lennard–Jones parameters, and the Fuller–Schettler–Giddings correlation D_AB = 1.00×10⁻³ T^1.75 (1/M_A + 1/M_B)^0.5 / [P (Σv_A^1/3 + Σv_B^1/3)²] with D in cm²/s and P in atm; note the T^1.75 and 1/P dependence. Prediction for liquids: Wilke–Chang, Hayduk–Laudie and Stokes–Einstein D = kT/(6πμr), with D proportional to T/μ. Give typical orders: gases 10⁻⁵, liquids 10⁻⁹, solids far smaller. State D_AB = D_BA for a binary gas.

figure.aria: A tree of ways to obtain a diffusivity, split into measurement and prediction for gases and for liquids, with the main named methods under each branch.

chapters.example: Estimate the diffusivity of CO2 in air at 300 K and 1 atm with the Fuller correlation. Data: M of CO2 = 44, M of air = 29, diffusion volume increments Σv = 26.9 for CO2 and 20.1 for air. Solution: (1/44 + 1/29) = 0.02273 + 0.03448 = 0.05721, whose square root is 0.2392. T^1.75 = 300^1.75 = 2.164×10⁴. The denominator is (26.9^(1/3) + 20.1^(1/3))² = (3.00 + 2.72)² = 32.7. So D_AB = 1.00×10⁻³×2.164×10⁴×0.2392/32.7 = 0.158 cm²/s, that is 1.58×10⁻⁵ m²/s, close to the measured value of about 1.6×10⁻⁵ m²/s.
chapters.trap: Feeding SI pressure and getting cm²/s out. The Fuller correlation wants P in atm and returns cm²/s; convert at the end and say which units you used.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.4 for the flux equations that a measurement is interpreted with; ideal gas law from Chapter 1.1.
chapters.leave: Dimensionless groups, mass transfer correlations and analogy equations to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: In a solid the diffusing atom hops between fixed sites or creeps through pores, so D is very small and rises steeply with temperature following an Arrhenius law.
chapters.depth: Mechanisms: interstitial diffusion of small atoms (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen in metals), vacancy or substitutional diffusion, grain-boundary and surface diffusion (fast paths), and pore or Knudsen diffusion for a gas in a porous solid. Fick's laws still hold with c as the concentration in the solid, and the surface concentration is usually set by solubility (Henry-type relation) rather than by the gas composition alone. Temperature dependence D = D₀ exp(−E/RT), with D₀ the pre-exponential factor (m²/s) and E the activation energy (J/mol). Give applications: carburizing and nitriding of steel, doping of silicon wafers, drying of wood, clay and food (moisture diffusion), polymer films in packaging, hydrogen through pipeline steel, membrane separation. Steady diffusion through a flat sheet: N_A = D (c_A1 − c_A2)/L. Only a few universities teach the Darken relation and the Kirkendall shift; mention them in one line and stop.

figure.aria: Diffusivity in a solid rising steeply with temperature, with the two worked points marked at 673 K and 773 K.

chapters.example: For a gas in a metal take D₀ = 2.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s and E = 60 kJ/mol; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). (a) Find D at 400 °C and at 500 °C. (b) A sheet 3 mm thick holds a steady concentration difference of 0.45 mol/m3 across it. Find the flux at 500 °C. Solution: (a) at 673 K, E/RT = 60000/(8.314×673) = 10.72, exp(−10.72) = 2.21×10⁻⁵, so D = 2.0×10⁻⁵×2.21×10⁻⁵ = 4.4×10⁻¹⁰ m²/s. At 773 K, E/RT = 9.34, exp(−9.34) = 8.8×10⁻⁵, so D = 1.76×10⁻⁹ m²/s. A 100 K rise multiplies D by 4. (b) N_A = D Δc/L = 1.76×10⁻⁹×0.45/0.003 = 2.6×10⁻⁷ mol/(m2·s).
chapters.trap: Using a gas-phase diffusivity of order 10⁻⁵ m²/s for a solid. Also forgetting the unit of E: kJ/mol must become J/mol before dividing by RT.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.3 for Fick's laws; Chapter 1.4 for the slab flux.
chapters.leave: Drying of solids and the drying rate curve to Unit 7. Membrane separations to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: With three or more species every pair has its own diffusivity, and the flux of one species depends on the gradients of all the others, which the Stefan–Maxwell equations describe and Wilke's formula makes usable for a dilute species.
chapters.depth: Define an n-component mixture and say when multicomponent treatment is needed: three or more species in comparable amounts, as in distillation of a multi-component feed, combustion, or a reformer gas. Write the Stefan–Maxwell equations for one dimension: dy_i/dz = Σ(y_i N_j − y_j N_i)/(c D_ij) over j ≠ i. Show that for n = 2 they reduce to Fick's law. Give Wilke's approximation for a species dilute in the rest: D_i,m = (1 − y_i)/Σ_{j≠i}(y_j/D_ij), used inside Fick's law as N_i = −c D_i,m dy_i/dz + y_i ΣN. Point out that D_i,m changes along the path because the composition changes, so fluxes must be integrated, not multiplied. Add one line that Knudsen diffusion in fine pores combines with molecular diffusion by the Bosanquet relation, which only a few universities teach.

figure.aria: Three species A, B and C joined by edges that carry the three binary diffusivities of the mixture.

chapters.example: A gas mixture has y_A = 0.10, y_B = 0.30 and y_C = 0.60, with binary diffusivities D_AB = 1.0×10⁻⁵, D_AC = 3.0×10⁻⁵ and D_BC = 2.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Find the effective diffusivity of A in the mixture by Wilke's formula. Solution: D_A,m = (1 − y_A)/(y_B/D_AB + y_C/D_AC) = 0.90/(0.30/1.0×10⁻⁵ + 0.60/3.0×10⁻⁵) = 0.90/(3.0×10⁴ + 2.0×10⁴) = 0.90/5.0×10⁴ = 1.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s. This value is used in Fick's law for A; it changes if the composition changes.
chapters.trap: Averaging binary diffusivities as y_A D_AB + y_B D_AC. Wilke's formula averages the resistances, 1/D, not D itself.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.3 and 1.4 for Fick's law and the binary flux forms.
chapters.leave: Multicomponent distillation and the Fenske–Underwood–Gilliland short cuts to Unit 4. Multicomponent absorption to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: When concentration changes with time, Fick's second law must be solved with the initial and boundary conditions of the shape, and the answers come as charts, series or error functions rather than one formula.
chapters.depth: Write the second law and set the three standard geometries: slab of half-thickness L, cylinder of radius R, sphere of radius R. Define the Fourier number for mass, Fo = D t/L², and the mass Biot number Bi_m = k_c L/D, which measures the surface resistance against the internal resistance. Give the semi-infinite result (c − c₀)/(c_s − c₀) = erfc(z/(2√(Dt))) for a surface held at c_s, and the first-term centre solution for a slab, C/C₀ = (4/π)exp(−π²Fo/4), valid for Fo > 0.2. Say that charts of C/C₀ against Fo for each Bi_m are used for the middle range. Add the membrane time lag t_lag = L²/(6D), the penetration idea for short contact times, and one line that a numerical solution is used when D varies. Cross-reference drying, which needs exactly these curves.

figure.aria: Dimensionless centre concentration of a slab against Fourier number, falling from the first-term curve and passing through the value 0.5 at Fo equal to 0.379.

chapters.example: A polymer sheet 20 mm thick, dry on both faces (surface concentration zero), starts with a uniform moisture concentration of 0.50 mol/m3. D = 2.0×10⁻¹⁰ m²/s. Find the time for the centre to fall to 0.25 mol/m3. Solution: C/C₀ = 0.5. For a slab with a fixed surface concentration and Fo > 0.2, use the first term: C/C₀ = (4/π)exp(−π²Fo/4), so 0.5 = 1.2732 exp(−2.4674 Fo), giving Fo = 0.379. The half-thickness is L = 10 mm = 0.010 m. Then t = Fo L²/D = 0.379×(0.010)²/2.0×10⁻¹⁰ = 1.9×10⁵ s, about 53 hours.
chapters.trap: Using the full thickness instead of the half-thickness for a slab dried from both faces, which gives a time four times too large. Also using the first-term formula below Fo = 0.2, where it is badly wrong.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.3 for the second law; Chapter 1.7 for diffusion in solids.
chapters.leave: Penetration and surface renewal theories, and mass transfer coefficients, to Unit 2. Drying rate curves and dryer design to Unit 7.
